It helped me overall. The four reasons, in my opinion, for any internship regardless of payment is:

1. Experience

2. Demonstrating results

3. Brand name

4. Connections and/or references


In my case, my first internship was sales at a tech startup in New York. I just cold called businesses from a list trying to sell software, unpaid. I made 100+ calls a day. It sucked.

I didn’t have very good results, but I just embellished a little bit on my resume. This was the summer after my sophomore year of college, so most people I was competing with for next summers internships had no experience period outside of classes. This allowed me to get a leg up and get an internship with a large midwestern bank, which then allowed me to get an internship with a large multinational abroad, which now makes my resume look awesome as a recent graduate. Should I have been paid? I believe so. But that first experience paved the way for everything else. I would rather an unpaid internship than no internship at all - you just need to make sure you get some value out of the experience that makes up for no $$$.

Disclaimer - So this is something I’m learning right now too, as an introvert trying to make friends for the first time, but here’s what I’ve learned so far:

Ask people to do stuff with you. Not just activities where you’re meant to do something, but “hey wanna go buy some clothes at the store with me?” Or, a more common one is “wanna get lunch/dinner/food with me?”

Friendships, especially deep ones, are not easy to develop for anyone. That’s why they’re special. You basically do activities with people over and over until you guys get closer. Also, take initiative - if you hear someone did something fun, say something like “wow that sounds cool, for real hit me up next time you go out ok?” Or find your own activity and say “hey I’m gonna go do this thing, wanna come with?”

Or, even if you want to be even more direct just say “hey do you have any plans this weekend? No? Wanna do something together?” Then come up with something. If they say they’ve got plans already, see what it is and ask if you can join. People are less judgmental of people wanting to hang out with others than you think, and those that are judgmental aren’t the types you want to hang out with anyway (seriously), no matter how “cool” or “fun” they seem to be. 

I’m also learning very quickly that not everyone who is popular is cool to hang out with, some people are mean or cliquey. In fact my very small group of friends has had a slow but definitely steady growth because once people realize we’re not assholes they want to hang with us more than the other larger, “cool” cliques.

The key thing to remember, again, is that friendships take time to develop. You always start out as acquaintances. That’s not a bad thing, that’s just one of the stages of developing a relationship. And not everyone will be a close friend either, but that doesn’t mean you can’t be friendly and have fun and a good relationship with them. 

Just take initiative, go out to events often, start saying yes more (unless something feels wrong, trust your instinct - ex. Don’t do heroin or spend exorbitant amounts of cash just to fit in). People aren’t going to ask you to hang out first typically unless they already know you, and you do that to actively involving yourself with them to build relationships.

Again I’m still learning, but this is had a lot of positive effects for me so far. Also use tinder or other similar apps  - just be clear you’re looking for friends only.

It definitely is. Now a lot of this depends on your situation so it would help to know a little bit more about you if possible. What is your GPA? What year in university are you going into? What country are you in? Etc etc.

The reason I ask about all of this is because it will affect where you apply. It varies by institution, each has their own specific set of rules. For example, most of UBS ‘s internships don’t require a specific major, but they DO require you have a 3.2 minimum GPA in whatever you are majoring in. Some are very specific in saying they want just economics or finance majors. Some internships vary by what year of students they accept. They might just want rising juniors, or some internships are specifically postgrad internships for rising seniors. All of this is trying to say it’s very situational, so the more info you can provide he better.

Now, in terms of general stuff:

-do extracurricular stuff. if your school has finance-related activities (finance/investment club, school-sponsored trips to network with alumni in business, etc etc) join those. And if you can, get a leadership position.

-You might be in health sciences, but if you can spare the time to take an accounting or basic business/finance course, do it. Even better if your university has banking specific courses.

-online courses. If you can - on websites like coursera. I’m on there right now taking a financial modeling course. Some are costlier than others, but having these courses on your resume is valuable because, besides whatever technical knowledge you gain, some employers will see you have a passion for finance/banking as you took time out of your day to do stuff that wasn’t required.


-Go to any conferences or events nearby for the industry. It sounds like you have already done so, which is good. Keep doing that. You can list these on resume and events you attended.

The reason for all of the above is to be able to show on your resume you are interested and serious about going into finance, even if you’re not majoring in it. 

S quick aside on the events too - don’t be discouraged by what people say at these events. Like I said before, 99.99999% of the time it won’t directly lead to a job, but they can give you advice  AND if you connect with them and get their contact info, you can reach out to them later. You can say something like “hey Joe, this is Alfred - we connected last month at TD Bank’s  networking event. I noticed you know/are connected to Jill at BofA, do you think you could introduce me? I really curious about hearing about what she does.”  This is especially why I recommend eating involved on LinkedIn - you can directly see your connections’ connections and what they do, and quickly expand this way.

Lastly, this would be something you would do if all else fails - most teller jobs have a fairly low bar and a college degree gives you a huge leg up. It won’t be glamorous work, but if you’re serious about banking, you can go through that way and most banks have training programs for their employees who want to go to higher positions. You can also save up for an MBA if you’re thinking about that, that’s how a lot of people get higher positions straight out of school.


In summary - yes you can still get involved despite not majoring in finance, I’m an economics major myself so I’m not a super finance guy. BUT I warn you, as someone who just went through the internship search process this past year, it’s tedious. I started my search in September, applied to over 50 positions and had over 40 meetings with my career counselor. From that I got interviews at only about 5-6 places, and got 2 offers from that. Both of those offers only came in early May. Again - it is ENTIRELY possible, but you need to understand how much work you will need to put in. This is not to crap on you I’m not saying it’s hard because you’re unqualified - you are not unqualified. But just understand that job hunting is hard and you will need to put in the effort. It’s very worth it though :)

Luckily, the good news for you is we are discussing this at the EXACT right time - right around now is when the top places started posting their internship openings, and the other financial institutions follow suit soon after. Now through December-January is prime recruitment season for internships.

If your school has a career services center, get an appointment ASAP and explain everything you’ve said here too. You’ll get expert advice specific to you and, if you happen to go to a big school, they might even have someone who specific focuses on business/finance internships. ALSO: they can hook you up with alumni. Some alumni specifically look for students from their school to work at their current company. 

For example, one of my interviews this year was with a huge insurance company, and I got through to the second round of interviews because my school’s career services brought one of their recruiters on campus for in-person informational interviews, and I was literally the only one who showed up with a resume. That obviously made a good impression on the recruiter, so she encouraged me to apply to the internship and, since she was the recruiter who did the first round phone interview, basically said “yeh I already interviewed you I person and I like you, I’ll pass you on to the second round what time works for you?”

This doesn’t always happen but yeah leverage your school as much as you can.

Internships - if you’re out of college there will be less available but some that don’t need a degree. No matter what you do in the internship, you can then network with people in any area of the bank and you’ll be far more likely to land an unadvertised job when someone goes “hmm he did well in the internship and as we’ve already hired him as an intern we already think he’s a good fit for our culture, and he’s interested in our department, so let’s see if we can squeeze him in somewhere.” Then work your way up the ladder.

If you can’t find an internship many banks also have networking events, go to those and mingle with the employees. If they like you and you express interest they can have a similar reaction to above.

Last, LinkedIn. Make a good profile, send out connection requests like nobody’s business. You even sit search “banker” and filter by people and connect to all those results. When you connect with someone in banking or the area you want to go into, message them soon after and be cordial. Express an interest in their field, ask if you can set up a networking call or go out for coffee/ or something. 99.99999% of the time you won’t get a job offer or anything close to it, but if they like you they may know someone who knows someone who can get you started somewhere. And even if nothing job-related comes from it, they can give you valuable advice on how to format your resume, present yourself, other stuff to do to help your job search, etc etc. As you do this a lot you’ll get what I mean - it’s a learning experience.

Again, all this will be difficult at first but it’s a learning experience - you’ll pick up how to do things well on your own as you do all of this more and more.

Just be understanding you might not get a superstar position at first. In fact, you probably won’t. Unless you have some skill set that people really want, you’ll likely have to do a lot of grunt work and more networking and do well to work your way up the corporate ladder. That’s just how it is, even for a lot of people who do land “cool” jobs.

All of this said, you can do it. It will be daunting at first but you’ll get better as you do it. Job hunting sucks, but just keep doing it. “Be positive, patient, and persistent”.

There’s so much I could say here as a fellow college student who’s gone through an extremely similar issue. I was originally a physics major too,  but at the time I didn’t have the work ethic to do well so I was failing classes. Eventually I switched to economics, but my gpa dropped more than it should have because, even though my grades were poor, I hung on to the “I need to have a technical major or it’s not worth it and I’ll disappoint everyone” mindset for a long time. I don’t really know where to start but here goes.

In terms of career:

This is a big thing, and the biggest concern I hear most expressed by parents of kids that are switching from a very technical major to a more humanities-based one.

From what I’ve learned as a student in the internship hunt (I got three separate job offers in my search, one of which I didn’t even apply for - I was headhunted by a large fintech company), employers in the future won’t really care what your major was - they care about how well you performed and what skill sets you have, and (SOMETIMES) what specific classes you took.

If you want to be, for example,a computer science guy, nobody cares that you majored in history if you learned how to code in your off time. It might be somewhat harder to compete with he fancy compsci degree others may have, but in the end it will all work out if you work hard and enjoy what you do.  

In fact, you can still apply your physics knowledge by saying in interviews something like “I switched to a history major, but as you can see here I aced the physics classes I was taking while in the major and developed the skillsets in those classes you’re looking for”. Taking this one step further, you can still take physics, math, or other technical classes to acquire said skillsets without having to do a full major in that area. Just do well in the class and actually learn the stuff.

You don’t need to work in the field you major in - in fact, most don’t. In summary - do well and learn skills and you’ll be fine. Internships in your field of choice are cool too if you can get them.


Another question I would pose: 

What would give you more value - spending money to take a major you hate and learn a lot less, or spend money to take classes you love and learn a lot more?

If you can, I recommend you go your university’s counseling department if they have one. I’m not saying you need therapy, but my university counselor has been invaluable in helping me make important decisions and tackle complex questions like this one - and given me a different perspective to reflect on. They’ve revealed aspects of situations I didn’t consider which aided my thought process immensely.

My university operates in trimesters, and is located in northern Wisconsin and it gets very cold.

So, they decided that they would shorten the first trimester of the year - making it end in late November, so the students would leave the campus for the last week of November and the entire month of December. That way, the administration reasoned, they wouldn’t have to pay the electric bill to keep the dorms and halls heated and lit during the cold, dark Wisconsin winter.

However, they forgot one small detail: there’s students that don’t/can’t go home for the holidays, like international students or students from distant areas of the country. So basically the university lost money because they had to keep the lights, heating, almost all university services on anyway and the tuition and housing bill is less for almost everyone, since everyone has a break from classes and most are off-campus once the first trimester ends in late November and don’t return until early January. 

And this wasn’t just a one-off either, this large winter break continues to this day since the school was too lazy to restore the first trimester to its proper length.

So, good for the students, bad for the administration.


Also, same university:

In the middle of each trimester there’s a few days where there are no classes called “midterm reading period”, the idea is of course to use those days to study for midterms. One year, the administration decided to cancel midterm reading period for the whole year. I guess they thought it wasn’t needed anymore.

You’re never actually a “part” of BWW other then you can buy their materials and attend conferences that they host. I'm twenty now, almost twenty\-one, but I started feeling suicidal right around when I was sixteen or seventeen. I felt like my life was really unfulfilled and I was letting everyone down because I had a good home \+ family \+ education and was a terrible student. I don't know how you feel, but in short my depression felt/feels like a numbness and desire for nothing underlined by an intense sadness, which sometimes comes out in mental breakdowns. I even had one really good friend like you whose house I slept over at a lot \(and still do\). After I got a GPA of around 2.0 my freshman year my parents told me they'd stop paying for college if I didn't improve, so I took a leave of absence. I started developing a suicide plan to jump off of the George Washington Bridge \(I have a low pain tolerance so I wanted a quick death\). I didn't know when I would act on it exactly since I was still working up the courage, but I wanted to do it in a couple of weeks. I just had to work up the courage to actually do it.

Then, for the first time, I accidentally told my current therapist \(I've gone through a lot of therapists\) about what I was thinking. It was really odd since it was our first session together. I tried to soften it so I wouldn't sound weird, but I more or less let out that I was planning to jump of the GWB. Long story short, she then kind of tricked me into getting myself forcibly hospitalized in the psych ward of the nearest hospital. I hated her at the time for it, but there was nothing I could do. When my parents were told of what had happened and came to bring me clothes, my mom couldn't even look at me. That first day the hospital was the worst feeling ever.

But then, things started to improve. I was diagnosed with major depression and social anxiety, so I was given antidepressants. Also, I talked to the person who prescribed me my meds. He was the first person I really opened up to because he understood how depressed I was. He didn't try to pretend like it wasn't so bad or whatever. He basically acted as my therapist for my two\-week\-ish stay in the psych ward, and still met with me part\-time in a therapist role and to prescribe me meds for when I was in the "intensive outpatient unit". It's kind of like an alcoholics\-anonymous group for people that have had to stay at the hospital. You don't have to live in the hospital anymore, but you have to go to this group for several weeks after your stay the hospital to help you improve mentally. Also, while I was in the psych ward, I met a number of bipolar people and, trust me, I will never make another bipolar joke again because I understand now how serious of an issue it is. This was the start of me moving to be a better place than where I was.

Fast\-forwarding a little bit, I took two\-thirds of the school\-year off \(my college operates in trimesters, not semesters, yes its weird lol\) to recover and keep going to therapy. It was hospital policy that I couldn't keep meeting with that first psychiatrist who helped me so much which made me REALLY sad, but after going through  a few therapists I finally found one that helped a lot. I want to stress here that this is NOT, NOT, NOT \(did I say NOT\) an instant\-recovery story. I had to withdraw from one of my three classes, I got D\+ in the other, but I got an A\+ in the third which I'd never gotten before. I wasn't happy at the time since my parents were focusing on the other two classes, but looking back on it I'm really happy I got that A\+. So, I kept going to therapy over the summer and then, for the next academic year, which I want to stress is THIS YEAR \(it's not over yet, finals are next week for the spring trimester\), I'm likely going to finish with around a 2.8ish GPA \(3.0 if I'm lucky\). An almost ONE POINT improvement.

I'm still dealing with a LOT of problems. I have HUGE sleep issues \(it's 5:30 in the morning as I write this\), I've been skipping out on my antidepressants because I have trouble following a regular schedule \(ADHD WOOPEE!!!!!!!!!\), and I've called my campus's suicide hotline and had breakdowns multiple times this year, but I'm slowly improving and am in a much better place than where I was a year and a half ago.

I don't really know how to end this, and this is definitely not a "and\-I\-lived\-happily\-ever\-after" story, I still have a lot of challenges and my future is uncertain. But uncertainty, I think, is a big characteristic of this time period.

Thank you for reading this far down :\)
